title: Multiply Strings
statement: Two non-negative whole numbers arrive as digit strings, each up to a couple of hundred digits long. Return their product, also as a digit string. Do not convert the inputs to a number type or use a big-integer library: do the multiplication digit by digit.

example.caption: 12 times 34. Each digit of 12 meets each digit of 34, and the four partial products land in four result slots.

idea.sentence: Digit i of the first number times digit j of the second lands in result slots i+j and i+j+1, so fill a result array of m+n slots and carry as you go.

jargon.plain: One position in the result array. Slot 0 is the leftmost digit of the product, slot m+n-1 the rightmost.
When a slot would hold 10 or more, keep the ones digit and push the tens digit one slot to the left.

watch.inputHint: Two digit strings, like "123" and "45". Keep them short (a product of about 3 by 2 digits fits the step cap).

compare.bruteLabel: Add num1 to itself num2 times
compare.optimalLabel: One multiply per pair of digits
compare.unit: operations (rough shape; repeated addition grows with the value, so exponentially in the digits)

rows.name: Repeated addition
rows.note: Adding num1 to itself num2 times is exponential in the number of digits. Useless for 200 digits.

rows.name: Grade-school multiplication
rows.note: Every digit pair is multiplied once and written into the result array.

fast.takeaway: This is long multiplication from school, with the carries written into an array. Faster methods like Karatsuba exist, but m x n is what interviews expect.

stages.title: Result slots
stages.note: An m-digit number times an n-digit number has at most m + n digits, so start with m + n zeros.

stages.title: Pick a digit of num1
stages.note: Walk the first number from its last digit to its first.

stages.title: Multiply and carry
stages.note: For each digit of the second number: p = product + the ones slot. Keep p % 10 in slot i+j+1 and add p / 10 to slot i+j.

stages.title: Trim and join
stages.note: The product may be one digit shorter than m + n, so skip leading zeros, but keep one digit so that 0 times 0 is 0.

edges.title: Zero times zero
edges.why: Both result slots stay 0. Trimming must stop at the last digit, or it would return an empty string.

edges.title: Zero times anything
edges.why: Three slots of 0. The product is shorter than m + n, so trim until only one 0 is left.

edges.title: All nines
edges.why: Every product is 81, the worst case for carries. Four slots are needed, and no leading zero is left to trim.

edges.title: Bigger than any integer
edges.why: A 64-bit integer holds about 19 digits. This case is exactly why the task forbids converting to numbers.

gotchas.text: Converting to numbers overflows. A 64-bit integer holds only about 19 digits, and a JS number is exact only up to 15 or 16. Keep each digit separate and carry by hand.
Place digits by index from the right: i+j+1 is the ones slot, i+j the tens slot. If you swap them, every carry lands one place too far right.
num1[i] is a one-character string. '7' * '8' works by coercion, but '7' + '8' gives '78'. Wrap each digit with Number(...) so the intent is clear and the plus never joins text.
res[i + j] += Math.floor(p / 10) can leave a slot at 10 or more for a moment. That is fine: the next pass writes that slot as p % 10 and carries again. Never print a slot before the loops end.

num1[i] is a byte, not a rune or a string. Digits are ASCII, so num1[i]-'0' is the digit value. Convert it to int before multiplying: a byte holds only 0 to 255, so product-plus-carry math done in bytes could wrap around.

recap.key: Digit i times digit j goes into slots i+j and i+j+1 of an (m+n)-slot result. Keep the ones digit, carry the tens left.
recap.complexity: Time O(m x n). Space O(m + n).
moves: Result array of m + n zeros
For each digit pair (from the right): p = a x b + res[i+j+1]
Skip leading zeros, keep one, join
